steps.title: How the Voyagers Borrowed Motion from Planets
steps.markdown:
Imagine planning a road trip in which each city helps propel you toward the next. That sounds impossible on Earth, but something similar made the Voyager journeys possible. A planet can redirect a passing spacecraft and give it extra speed without the spacecraft firing a large engine. The maneuver is called a **gravity assist**, and its secret is that planets are moving.

NASA launched Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 in 1977 to explore Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 2 eventually continued to Uranus and Neptune. Their routes exploited a rare arrangement of the outer planets that allowed successive encounters: each flyby could prepare the spacecraft for another destination. [NASA’s planetary voyage overview](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/planetary-voyage/)

The central idea is simple, although its mechanism takes a little unpacking: **gravity can transfer some of a planet’s orbital energy to a spacecraft by bending its path.** Here, orbital energy means the energy associated with an object’s motion and position as it travels around another body.

Start with the launch. A rocket gives a spacecraft its initial motion, but reaching one planet does not automatically provide enough energy to reach every planet beyond it. NASA explains that the Voyagers’ launch vehicles supplied enough energy to reach Jupiter’s distance. Without a suitably timed encounter with Jupiter, their initial paths would have carried them outward and then back toward the Sun. [NASA’s trajectory explanation](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/basics-of-space-flight/chapter4-1/)

Jupiter therefore served as both a destination and a means of continuing the journey. To understand how, first imagine watching the encounter from alongside Jupiter.

As Voyager approaches, Jupiter’s gravity pulls it inward. The spacecraft speeds up, much as a bicycle speeds up while rolling down into a valley. Its existing sideways motion carries it past the planet rather than into it. Gravity continuously bends its trajectory—the path it follows through space.

After closest approach, Voyager travels away from Jupiter and slows as it climbs out of the planet’s gravitational influence. In an idealized encounter, measured relative to Jupiter and sufficiently far away on either side, its outgoing speed equals its incoming speed. Its direction, however, has changed. The valley analogy helps explain the temporary acceleration: ignore friction, and a cyclist returning to the original height gives back the speed gained downhill. [NASA’s gravity assist primer](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/basics-of-space-flight/primer/)

That seems to leave us with a puzzle. If the spacecraft gives back the speed it gained, where does the lasting boost come from?

Now change your viewpoint. Watch from a position where you measure motion relative to the Sun. Jupiter is moving around the Sun throughout the encounter. The spacecraft’s motion relative to Jupiter must be combined with Jupiter’s own motion. Because the flyby changes the spacecraft’s direction, that combination can produce a greater outgoing speed relative to the Sun. The planet’s motion and the bending of the path work together. [NASA’s gravity assist primer](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/basics-of-space-flight/primer/)

A familiar example makes the importance of viewpoint easier to grasp. Walk toward the front of a moving train. Someone inside measures your walking speed relative to the carriage; someone standing beside the track measures that walking motion combined with the train’s motion. Turn and walk toward the rear, and your walking speed inside can remain unchanged while your speed relative to the ground changes.

This walking example illustrates how direction affects combined motion. The spacecraft’s actual turn is produced by gravity, and the energy accounting is physical: Voyager pulls gravitationally on Jupiter while Jupiter pulls on Voyager. When the spacecraft gains orbital energy, the planet loses a corresponding amount. Jupiter’s enormous mass makes its change imperceptibly small compared with the spacecraft’s useful gain. A differently arranged flyby can instead slow a spacecraft relative to the Sun. [NASA’s trajectory explanation](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/basics-of-space-flight/chapter4-1/)

Consider Voyager 2’s Jupiter encounter as a concrete example. It passed closest to Jupiter on July 9, 1979. That encounter was planned partly to preserve later planetary visits. After a course correction following closest approach, it continued toward Saturn, which it reached in August 1981. The gravity assist supplied the major change in its onward trajectory; navigation maneuvers refined the route. [NASA’s Voyager 2 mission history](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/voyager-2/)

Saturn then helped send Voyager 2 toward Uranus, whose encounter prepared its passage to Neptune. Voyager 2 reached Uranus in January 1986 and Neptune in August 1989. These were connected stages of one carefully arranged journey: the conditions at an earlier encounter helped determine which later encounters were possible. [NASA’s Voyager 2 mission history](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/voyager-2/)

Timing was therefore as important as speed. A spacecraft must meet a planet where the planet will be when it arrives. The favorable Voyager arrangement recurs roughly every 175 years; “alignment” here means useful orbital geometry, rather than requiring all four planets to stand in a straight row. NASA studied more than 10,000 trajectories before selecting the two Voyager routes. [NASA’s planetary voyage overview](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/planetary-voyage/)

Those routes also show that a gravity assist is a steering decision. Voyager 1’s Saturn encounter prioritized a close passage by Titan, Saturn’s largest moon, and sent the spacecraft northward out of the plane in which most planets orbit. Voyager 2’s Saturn route preserved the onward journey to Uranus. The same planet could support different scientific itineraries through different encounter geometry. [NASA’s planetary voyage overview](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/planetary-voyage/)

Our explanation simplifies the calculation by considering a planet-centered view during the flyby and a Sun-centered view of the wider journey. Real navigation must account for planets continually changing position and must refine the spacecraft’s approach. Modern NASA navigators still use this combination of careful geometry, energy exchange, and trajectory corrections. [JPL’s explanation of gravity assist navigation](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/home/news/nasas-europa-clipper-uses-mars-to-go-the-distance/)

The Voyagers’ great travel advantage came from treating moving planets as part of the transportation system. Gravity supplied the connection, planetary motion supplied the available energy, and precise timing made the exchange useful.
steps.takeaway: A gravity assist bends a spacecraft’s path around a moving planet, allowing it to gain orbital energy and reach its next destination with far less propulsion.
steps.next: How Voyager sends scientific measurements to Earth across billions of kilometers using radio waves and the Deep Space Network.
steps.summary: Voyager’s planetary journeys depended on gravity assists. A flyby changes the spacecraft’s direction while leaving its distant incoming and outgoing speeds approximately equal relative to the planet. Relative to the Sun, the moving planet can transfer orbital energy to the spacecraft. Carefully timed encounters connected Voyager 2’s visits to Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

diagram.caption: Stages of one speed-increasing gravity assist, following the same spacecraft throughout. Incoming and outgoing speeds are compared far from the planet; this conceptual picture simplifies the Sun’s influence and omits navigation corrections.

nodes.label: Timed approach
nodes.detail: The spacecraft approaches a planet moving around the Sun.

nodes.label: Inward acceleration
nodes.detail: The planet’s gravity speeds up the spacecraft and bends its path.

nodes.label: Outward climb
nodes.detail: The spacecraft slows relative to the planet as it departs in a new direction.

nodes.label: Onward journey
nodes.detail: Its speed relative to the Sun is greater, with energy transferred from the planet’s orbit.
